title: The Gender Gap in AI
source_used: Pew Research Center short read (full text)
key_facts: Survey of 5,119 US adults, 17 to 23 Feb 2026, from Pew's American Trends Panel; the short read is an excerpt of a broader June 2026 study.
Women are about twice as likely to say AI will have a negative impact on them personally over the next 20 years than a positive one (33% vs 17%); men are more evenly split.
43% of women expect AI to affect society negatively.
68% of women versus 58% of men say AI is moving too fast.
35% of men say chatbots help their productivity versus 25% of women.
Men are more likely to use Copilot (22% vs 13%); ChatGPT use is identical for men and women.
Just over half of men have heard a lot about AI versus 41% of women; 22% of men and 15% of women are extremely or very confident using chatbots.
quote_evidence: Men report using chatbots more regularly than women and are more likely to turn to them for a variety of things, including work.
In our new survey, women are about twice as likely to say AI will have a negative impact on them personally over the next 20 years than a positive one (33% vs. 17%).
Majorities of Americans believe AI is moving too fast, but women are more likely than men to say this (68% vs. 58%).
why_it_matters_hint: Pew's survey shows a consistent gender gap in how Americans use and view AI.
